newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: GOVERNMENT SEALS UBS DEAL ON TELECOM SALE.
newsitem.headline: GOVERNMENT SEALS UBS DEAL ON TELECOM SALE.

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) on Tuesday signed a deal with Lithuania to become the government's adviser in the sale of the country's state-owned telecommunications monopoly.

Under the deal, UBS and the consortium it leads will draw up the privatisation programme and help write the regulatory framework under which Lithuanian Telecom will operate after it is delivered into private hands next year.
"What we aim at is the liberalisation of the telecommunications market," Communications Minister Rimantas Pleikys told reporters after the signing of the agreement.
Officials would not say how much UBS was getting for its services or how much they thought Lithuanian Telecom would bring into state coffers.
"The final price and the only one that matters is the one that results from a competitive tender process," said Michael Phair, UBS global head of telecoms investment banking.
The privatisation programme is expected to be complete in late autumn, after which a three-stage selection process is expected to take place to chose the Telecom investor, Phair said.

Applicants will have to pass a pre-qualification test to reach stage two, when they will receive an information memorandum, meet with government and Telecom officials and submit a non-binding indicator bid, Phair said.

Phair said stage three will probably include a further narrowing of candidates, more detailed information on Telecom, development of the contractual framework for the sale of shares and the final bids.
Officials expect the final sale to be finalised by the end of March.
"We hope to drink a glass of champagne on April 1," Pleikys said.
Pleikys said that whoever buys into Lithuanian Telecom will be investing into a monopoly that could last until 2003, although it will be tempered by price caps and safeguards for the government.
"For the long-term strategic importance of the telecommunications sector, the government will retain a golden share," Phair said.

The investor is also expected to face obligations to build up the telecommunications network, improve the quality of service and create new ones, said Kiron Sarkar, a representative of CIBC Wood Gundy, a member of the UBS consortium.
"So the government will have some protections and the investor will have some obligations imposed on it after privatisation," Sarkar said.
